variants.title: Configure the client
variants.context: Configure each client from where its secrets can live: server web apps enable Client authentication, Standard flow, and PKCE S256; SPAs and native apps disable Client authentication, require PKCE, register exact redirects, and keep Implicit and Direct access grants off; machine services enable Client authentication and Service account roles.
variants.prompt: A React single-page app is registered in Keycloak. Which settings?
options: Client authentication Off, Standard flow On, PKCE S256 required, exact redirect URIs, Implicit and Direct access grants Off.
Client authentication On with the secret in the bundle.
optionFeedback: Distributed code cannot protect a shared secret.
A secret in the bundle is public.
Implicit is unsuitable for new designs.
variants.explanation: Public clients rely on PKCE and exact redirects.

variants.prompt: A backend service calls an API with no user. Which settings?
options: Client authentication On, Service account roles On, browser and password flows Off.
optionFeedback: The workload authenticates as itself with only the roles it needs.
Standard flow needs a user.
Password grants are unsuitable.
variants.hint: Is there a browser or a user?
variants.explanation: Disable capabilities the workload never uses.

variants.prompt: A client registers a wildcard redirect https://*.example.com/*. What is the risk?
options: Tokens or codes can be sent to any matching host; register specific redirect URIs.
optionFeedback: Wildcards are not exact matching.
Redirect control is a security boundary.
Performance is unrelated.
variants.hint: Which hosts could receive the code?

variants.title: Trace the login
variants.context: A browser login is a sequence of boundaries: start authorization with state and a PKCE verifier; Keycloak establishes identity through an SSO session or the realm’s flow; the client redeems the code at the token endpoint; the client validates the ID token and the API independently validates the access token.
variants.prompt: A user signs into a server-rendered app through Keycloak. Put the boundaries in order.

items.text: The app creates transaction state and a PKCE verifier, then redirects to the realm’s authorization endpoint with an exact callback.
Keycloak reuses an eligible SSO session or runs the realm’s authentication flow.
The client sends the one-time code and verifier to the token endpoint; a confidential client also authenticates.
The client validates the ID token; the API independently validates the access token’s signature, issuer, audience, expiry, and scope.

variants.hint: The API never trusts the client’s validation.
variants.explanation: Start → establish identity → redeem → enforce. Keep the responsibilities separate.

variants.title: Trace the login
variants.context: A browser login is a sequence of boundaries: start authorization with state and a PKCE verifier; Keycloak establishes identity through an SSO session or the realm’s flow; the client redeems the code at the token endpoint; the client validates the ID token and the API independently validates the access token.
variants.prompt: Login is brokered to an external identity provider. Put the steps in order.

items.text: The app starts authorization with state and PKCE.
Keycloak brokers the user to the external provider and maps the result into its realm identity.
The code is redeemed at Keycloak’s token endpoint.
The app validates the ID token and the API validates the access token.

variants.hint: Brokering happens inside the identity step; the app’s protocol contract is unchanged.
variants.explanation: Keycloak presents one protocol contract regardless of identity source.

variants.title: Trace the login
variants.context: A browser login is a sequence of boundaries: start authorization with state and a PKCE verifier; Keycloak establishes identity through an SSO session or the realm’s flow; the client redeems the code at the token endpoint; the client validates the ID token and the API independently validates the access token.
variants.prompt: A second app in the same realm is opened. Put the steps in order.

items.text: The second app starts its own authorization transaction.
Keycloak reuses the existing SSO session without a new credential prompt.
The second app redeems its own code.
The second app and its API validate their own tokens.

variants.hint: SSO reuses the session, not the tokens.
variants.explanation: Each client gets its own tokens; the session is what is shared.

variants.title: Use each token correctly
variants.context: ID token: identity assertion for the client. Access token: credential for a resource server that must reject other audiences. Refresh token: used only at the token endpoint. Keycloak session: server-side SSO continuity, distinct from token expiry.
variants.prompt: A client sends its ID token as the Authorization bearer to an API. What is wrong?
options: The ID token is an identity assertion for the client, not the API’s credential; use the access token.
It should send the refresh token.
optionFeedback: Do not merge the token roles.
The API needs a token minted for its audience.
Refresh tokens never go to APIs.
variants.explanation: Applications must use each token only for its intended audience.

variants.title: Use each token correctly
variants.context: ID token: identity assertion for the client. Access token: credential for a resource server that must reject other audiences. Refresh token: used only at the token endpoint. Keycloak session: server-side SSO continuity, distinct from token expiry.
variants.prompt: An access token minted for the billing API is presented to the orders API. What should happen?
options: The orders API rejects it because the audience does not name it.
optionFeedback: Audience restriction is enforced per resource server.
Realm membership is not audience.
User identity does not change the audience.
variants.hint: Which audience is in the token?
variants.explanation: The API must reject a token minted for another audience.

variants.title: Use each token correctly
variants.context: ID token: identity assertion for the client. Access token: credential for a resource server that must reject other audiences. Refresh token: used only at the token endpoint. Keycloak session: server-side SSO continuity, distinct from token expiry.
variants.prompt: Where may a refresh token be used?
options: Only at the token endpoint, never sent to APIs or placed in URLs and logs.
optionFeedback: It obtains replacement tokens.
APIs must never see it.
URLs leak into logs and history.

variants.title: Use the right boundary
variants.context: A realm owns users, clients, roles, sessions, flows, and signing keys; the master realm administers the server. Keycloak issues roles and claims but does not replace application authorization.
variants.prompt: Application users are being created in the master realm. What is wrong?
options: The master realm administers the server; application identities belong in purpose-built realms.
optionFeedback: Keep server administration separate from application identity.
master is the administrative realm.
Groups are inside a realm, not a substitute for one.
variants.explanation: Realms are the identity and key boundary.

variants.title: Use the right boundary
variants.context: A realm owns users, clients, roles, sessions, flows, and signing keys; the master realm administers the server. Keycloak issues roles and claims but does not replace application authorization.
variants.prompt: A valid token carries role orders:read. May the API return any order?
options: No. The API must still enforce ownership, tenant boundaries, and business rules.
optionFeedback: Keycloak does not replace application authorization.
A role is not object-level permission.
Realm membership is not ownership.
variants.hint: What does a role say about a specific object?
variants.explanation: A valid token is not permission to access every object.

variants.title: Use the right boundary
variants.context: A realm owns users, clients, roles, sessions, flows, and signing keys; the master realm administers the server. Keycloak issues roles and claims but does not replace application authorization.
variants.prompt: Two customers need separate signing keys, login policies, and administrators. Which construct?
optionFeedback: Realms own keys, policy, and administration.
Scopes shape claims, not isolation.
Groups organize users inside one realm.
variants.explanation: Clients, groups, roles, and scopes are not interchangeable tenant-isolation mechanisms.

variants.title: Count the logins
variants.context: One realm SSO session can serve several clients; separate realms have separate sessions and keys. Access tokens are short-lived and refreshed against the session.
variants.prompt: Three applications are clients of one realm. A user opens all three in one browser session. How many credential prompts?
variants.hint: One realm session serves several clients.
variants.explanation: One login; the SSO session is reused by the other two clients.

mistakes.feedback: The first application still needs a login.

variants.title: Count the logins
variants.context: One realm SSO session can serve several clients; separate realms have separate sessions and keys. Access tokens are short-lived and refreshed against the session.
variants.prompt: The same three applications are split across three separate realms. How many credential prompts?
variants.explanation: Each realm has its own session and keys, so three logins.

variants.title: Count the logins
variants.context: One realm SSO session can serve several clients; separate realms have separate sessions and keys. Access tokens are short-lived and refreshed against the session.
variants.prompt: Access tokens last 5 minutes and the session lasts 8 hours. At most how many access-token refreshes can one client perform in that session?
variants.hint: Divide the session length by the token lifetime.
variants.explanation: 480 minutes ÷ 5 = 96 tokens over the session, each obtained without a new login.
